records.title: Does marriage and relationship education work? A meta-analytic study.
records.journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
records.design: Meta-analysis (86 reports, 117 studies, >500 effect sizes)
records.population_setting: Mostly US/Western MRE program participants; predominantly White, middle-class samples
records.key_finding: Relationship-quality effect sizes for experimental studies ranged d=.30-.36 and communication-skills effects d=.43-.45; moderate-dosage programs outperformed low-dosage; the authors flag that racial/ethnic and economic diversity was too thin to draw reliable conclusions for disadvantaged couples, and that outcomes policymakers care about (relationship stability, aggression) were rarely measured.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Foundational MRE effectiveness base rate. Directly relevant to the FAILURE CRITERION: shows conventional MRE literature has historically measured satisfaction/communication, not coercion recognition or safe help-seeking -- supports T-PHE's premise that a governance/decision-control layer measures something existing MRE evidence has not captured (complicates P1/P6 by showing the evidence gap T-PHE claims to address is real).
records.evidence_level: Meta-analysis of RCTs/quasi-experiments (high on communication/satisfaction outcomes; silent on safety outcomes)

records.title: Exploring programmatic moderators of the effectiveness of marriage and relationship education programs: a meta-analytic study.
records.design: Meta-analysis (148 evaluation reports)
records.population_setting: Mixed university/laboratory and religious-setting MRE programs, largely US
records.key_finding: Moderate-dosage programs (9-20 contact hours) had stronger effects than low-dosage (1-8 hours); a communication-skills emphasis strengthened communication outcomes but not satisfaction; no evidence that formal institutionalization (manuals, trainer certification) improved effects, and no significant difference between religious-setting and university/laboratory delivery.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant to P1 (governance layer vs. content dose) and the religious-setting question directly germane to a TIMA/FIMA programme: dosage/format moderators mattered more than institutional formality or religious vs secular venue in this meta-analytic evidence -- neither strongly supports nor refutes a specific governance-layer effect, since no P1-type 'decision-control' variable was ever coded.

records.title: How effective are ACF-funded couple relationship education programs? A meta-analytic study.
records.design: Meta-analysis (32 control-group studies + 19 one-group pre-post studies)
records.population_setting: US lower-income couples/individuals enrolled in federally funded (ACF Healthy Marriage and Relationship Education) CRE programs
records.key_finding: Small but significant effects for relationship quality (d=.114), relationship skills (d=.132), mental health (d=.074) and coparenting (d=.033); effects on relationship stability, parenting and child well-being were non-significant.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports the FAILURE CRITERION logic: a large, well-funded government MRE effort shows small quality/skills gains but null effects on stability -- exactly the kind of pattern (soft-outcome movement without the harder outcome) T-PHE's failure criterion is designed to catch if applied to decision-control/coercion-recognition outcomes instead.

records.title: A randomized clinical trial of the effectiveness of premarital intervention: moderators of divorce outcomes.
records.design: Randomized controlled trial (couples via religious organizations randomized to PREP vs. naturally occurring premarital services; n=44/66/83)
records.population_setting: US couples marrying through religious organizations, 8-year follow-up on divorce
records.key_finding: No overall difference in divorce rates between PREP (clergy-delivered or professional-delivered) and usual premarital services; couples with higher premarital negative-communication observed pre-intervention were MORE likely to divorce if given PREP, while low-negativity couples benefited; a premarital history of physical aggression showed a similar (marginally significant) harmful-moderation pattern.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Complicates and partially supports T-PHE. It is a key evidence source for the STOP RULE / P4 logic: standard joint-couple relationship education can worsen outcomes for couples with pre-existing negative communication or aggression -- exactly the population the STOP RULE and coercion-screening safeguard are meant to route away from ordinary joint education. Also complicates P1/failure criterion: a rigorously delivered, faith-setting RCT of premarital education found no divorce-rate benefit overall, i.e. conventional-outcome success is not guaranteed even with religious-organization delivery.

records.title: Risk moderates the outcome of relationship education: a randomized controlled trial.
records.journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
records.design: RCT (N=130 engaged/newlywed couples randomized to 1 of 3 relationship-education programs, 3-year follow-up)
records.population_setting: US engaged and newlywed couples
records.key_finding: Couples with acute baseline concerns, including higher physical aggression and alcohol use, benefited LESS from relationship-education intervention than couples without these concerns; couples with high baseline satisfaction/commitment actually declined faster in satisfaction under an intensive skill-based intervention versus a low-intensity one.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports the STOP RULE (P4) and bounded-authority safeguard: this RCT is empirical evidence that undifferentiated relationship-skills intervention is not uniformly beneficial and can be counterproductive for higher-risk couples (aggression, substance use), reinforcing the case for a screening/stop mechanism before joint work rather than one-size-fits-all joint education.

records.title: Does premarital education decrease or increase couples' later help-seeking?
records.design: Cross-sectional survey study (N=2,126 married individuals)
records.population_setting: US married adults, general population sample
records.key_finding: Contrary to the assumption that premarital education reduces later need for counseling, receiving premarital education covaried with an INCREASED likelihood of later couples counseling (a 'gateway' effect), with the association stronger among African Americans and those with lower income/education.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly relevant to P2 (private channel making concerns visible) and the safe help-seeking outcome domain in the FAILURE CRITERION: empirical evidence that premarital education can function as a gateway that increases later formal help-seeking rather than substituting for it -- supports the plausibility that a T-PHE-style programme could raise help-seeking as an intended (not a failure) outcome, and is directly usable evidence for the referral-quality proposition (P5).
records.evidence_level: Cross-sectional survey, self-report; associative not causal

records.title: Barriers and facilitators of relationship help-seeking among low-income couples.
records.design: Cross-sectional self-report study (N=231 ethnically diverse newlywed couples in low-income neighborhoods)
records.population_setting: US low-income newlywed couples
records.key_finding: Top perceived barriers to seeking couple therapy were cost and uncertainty about where to go for help; direct experience with premarital education (or indirect experience via a social-network member's couple therapy) was associated with reduced barriers and greater likelihood of subsequently seeking therapy.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P2/P5 (private-channel visibility, referral quality = timeliness + accessibility + follow-through): identifies 'not knowing where to go' as a leading real-world barrier, which is precisely what an accountable-referral safeguard is designed to close; usable evidence base for why referral pathway design matters independent of content quality.

records.title: The role of leaders' working alliance in premarital education.
records.design: RCT sub-analysis (31 leaders training 118 couples/236 attendees in a PREP trial)
records.population_setting: US couples in a randomized PREP trial, multiple facilitators
records.key_finding: Relationship outcomes varied significantly by which leader delivered the training; facilitators' aggregated working-alliance quality (as rated by attendees) predicted change in observed communication and relationship satisfaction, over and above curriculum content itself.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant to dignity-and-consent and cultural-intelligibility safeguards and to P3: shows facilitator relational quality, not just curriculum content, drives outcomes -- supports the T-PHE premise that governance/process factors (who delivers, how) matter as much as content, and is a caution that programme fidelity depends on facilitator training/alliance, which T-PHE would need to operationalize for its own safeguards to be more than aspirational.

records.title: Revising Premarital Relationship Interventions for the Next Generation.
records.journal: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy
records.design: Narrative review/position paper
records.population_setting: General discussion of contemporary premarital-education practice, US-centric
records.key_finding: Reviews social trends (individualism/commitment ambivalence, changing marriage attitudes, premarital relationship histories, media environment) and argues current premarital interventions need updated content and structure to remain relevant to engaged couples today; offers four proposals for redesigning premarital interventions.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports the conceptual-synthesis framing of T-PHE itself (P1, P7): an independent call from within the MRE field for programme redesign and modernization, i.e., precedent for treating premarital education as needing structural/governance revision rather than only content updates -- but is itself non-empirical (opinion/review), so provides conceptual not evidentiary support.
records.evidence_level: Narrative review / expert opinion (no primary data)

records.title: Can marriage education mitigate the risks associated with premarital cohabitation?
records.design: RCT / secondary analysis (PREP for married couples in the U.S. Army, N=662 couples)
records.population_setting: US Army married couples
records.key_finding: Precommitment cohabitation (cohabiting before a mutual commitment to marry) was associated with lower marital satisfaction/dedication and higher divorce by 2-year follow-up in the control group, but this risk was NOT apparent in the PREP intervention group -- i.e., the education program appeared to buffer a known risk factor.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Complicates the FAILURE CRITERION in a useful way: this is exactly the kind of study T-PHE would need to be cautious about generalizing from -- it shows conventional relationship-education content CAN buffer a specific relational risk factor (cohabitation-associated distress) on conventional outcomes (satisfaction, divorce), which supports the plausibility that content-only programmes have real protective value, a nuance T-PHE's framework should not erase even while insisting content alone is insufficient for coercion/safety outcomes.
records.evidence_level: RCT / secondary analysis of trial data

records.title: 10-Year Study of Christian Church Support for Domestic Violence Victims: 2005-2015.
records.design: Repeated cross-sectional survey (convenience sample of Upper-Midwest US congregations, 2005 and 2015)
records.population_setting: Christian clergy and congregation members, US
records.key_finding: Faith commitments led some domestic-violence victims to endure abuse rather than compromise their faith by leaving; over 10 years, congregational support for victims changed slowly; clergy wanted more training in counseling and speaking about domestic violence, and felt comfortable making referrals but not necessarily providing direct DV counseling themselves.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports the STOP RULE and bounded-authority-and-referral safeguard (P4/P5): faith-based settings can inadvertently keep victims in danger when religious framing discourages leaving, and clergy themselves report needing referral pathways rather than attempting DV counseling directly -- strong real-world grounding for why joint faith-based marriage-preparation work must stop and refer, not proceed, when coercion/violence is suspected.

records.title: Culturally specific treatment for partner-abusive Latino men: a qualitative study to identify and implement program components.
records.design: Qualitative study (demographic survey + qualitative interviews) informing program design
records.population_setting: Latino immigrant men who are intimate-partner-violence perpetrators, Southern California
records.key_finding: A culturally specific, Spanish-language program integrating gender roles, immigration/discrimination context, marital sexual abuse, and spirituality was seen by participants as more relevant; the study explicitly frames cultural sensitivity as compatible with, not a substitute for, perpetrator accountability.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant to P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if it does not override consent/safety): this is evidence for the general design principle that culturally specific adaptation of violence-related intervention content is feasible and valued by participants WITHOUT diminishing accountability -- supports the T-PHE claim that cultural intelligibility and non-negotiable safety/accountability can coexist, though this study concerns perpetrator treatment, not premarital education, so applicability to T-PHE's couple-education context is indirect.
records.evidence_level: Qualitative study (program-development evidence, not outcome trial)

records.title: Prevention of marital dysfunction: behavioral approaches and beyond.
records.design: Narrative review of 13 program-evaluation studies
records.population_setting: General review of behaviorally oriented marriage-preparation programs, mostly US
records.key_finding: Behaviorally oriented, skills-based marriage-preparation programs across 13 reviewed studies showed evidence of producing behavioral changes that may help prevent marital dysfunction, though program-evaluation methodology at the time was described as only modestly improved and needing further rigor.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Historical evidence base for P6 (conventional success can coexist with failure): an early review already flagged methodological weakness in outcome measurement for marriage-preparation programs, i.e., the evidentiary gap T-PHE's failure criterion targets (measuring only satisfaction/skills, not coercion-recognition/safety) has been a recognized limitation in the field for decades, not a new critique invented by T-PHE.

records.title: Improving practice in marriage preparation.
records.design: Narrative review
records.population_setting: General review of marriage-preparation program practice, US
records.key_finding: Reviews two decades of research on marriage-preparation programs and gives design recommendations covering needs assessment, timing/duration, format, content, provider characteristics, and promotion; does not report new outcome data.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Background/context support for P7 (repairability) and overall programme-design literature: establishes needs assessment and provider characteristics as long-recognized levers for programme quality, consistent with T-PHE's emphasis on governance and safeguard design rather than content alone, but is descriptive/prescriptive, not an outcome evaluation.
records.evidence_level: Narrative review / practice guidance (no primary outcome data)

records.title: Changes in premarital counseling as related to older cohorts of married couples.
records.design: Retrospective cohort survey (N=256 current/former members of a Christian denomination)
records.population_setting: Members of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), US
records.key_finding: Over successive marriage cohorts, premarital counseling availability, voluntariness, and duration increased, but self-reported effectiveness of premarital counseling did not significantly change across cohorts -- possibly because marital challenges grew in complexity at a comparable rate.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports the FAILURE CRITERION logic historically: increased 'dose' and formalization of faith-based premarital counseling over time did not translate into perceived improvement in effectiveness, an early empirical parallel to T-PHE's claim that conventional programme growth (attendance, hours) can occur without improvement on the outcomes that matter.

records.title: Videoconferencing Delivery of the Seoul Premarital Education Program During COVID-19: A Quasi-experimental Study Using Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting.
records.design: Quasi-experimental study with inverse probability of treatment weighting (weighted N=291 women, 228 men)
records.population_setting: Couples in a city-wide (Seoul) premarital education program, South Korea, during COVID-19
records.key_finding: Videoconferencing delivery of the Seoul Premarital Education Program (S-PEP) was associated with increased marital readiness for both men and women, and with increased relationship confidence and satisfaction for women specifically.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant background for delivery-format questions (not directly Muslim/Thai context, but a non-Western, government-run premarital program) and for P1: like the ACF and Hawkins meta-analyses, measures only readiness/confidence/satisfaction, not decision control, coercion recognition, or safe help-seeking -- again illustrating the FAILURE CRITERION's evidentiary gap rather than contradicting T-PHE.

records.title: Premarital intervention based on attachment and differentiation improves communication and conflict management in Iranian couples.
records.design: Quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control-group study (N=40, 20 couples: 10 experimental, 10 control)
records.population_setting: Engaged couples at a university-affiliated counseling center, Iran (collectivist-society context)
records.key_finding: An 8-10 session attachment/differentiation-based premarital intervention produced significant post-intervention improvements in integrating, obliging and compromising communication styles and reduced avoidance/dominating styles (MANCOVA F=8.73-42.16, p<.01-.001) versus no-treatment control.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant comparator from a Muslim-majority, collectivist-culture setting close to T-PHE's own context: demonstrates conventional communication/conflict-skills gains are achievable in a culturally analogous population, again on process outcomes (communication style) rather than decision-control, coercion-recognition, or safe help-seeking -- useful as a 'what conventional success looks like' contrast case for the FAILURE CRITERION, and note the very small sample (n=20 couples) limits generalizability.

records.title: Cultural adaptation and pilot evaluation of the Couple Learning Program (CLP) among young Turkish couples: A mixed-method study.
records.design: Pilot randomized controlled trial, mixed methods (N=8 couples primary phase + 2 couples feasibility phase)
records.population_setting: Young premarital couples, Turkey (culturally adapted European program)
records.key_finding: A culturally adapted, 6-session Couple Learning Program produced significant improvements in conflict-resolution strategies (exit, voice, neglect dimensions) with relationship satisfaction improving only at follow-up (not immediately post-intervention); participants rated the culturally adapted program as relevant and acceptable.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly relevant to P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture does not override consent/safety): a rare pilot RCT of a Western-origin couple program culturally adapted for a Muslim-majority country, demonstrating feasibility and acceptability of cultural adaptation -- supports P3's premise that tailoring can improve engagement, though the extremely small pilot sample (8 couples) means this is preliminary feasibility evidence, not a powered effectiveness trial, and it still measures only communication/satisfaction, not safety or decision-control outcomes.
records.evidence_level: Pilot RCT, very small sample (feasibility-level evidence)

records.title: Perceived need of information and education about conception preparedness (CP) among engaged and soon to be married couples: a qualitative survey.
records.design: Qualitative descriptive study (focus group discussions, N=40 engaged couples)
records.population_setting: Engaged couples recruited at premarital counseling sites (churches, sector administration offices), Rwanda
records.key_finding: Engaged couples identified specific unmet information/education needs regarding conception preparedness, with premarital counseling sites (including religious venues) identified as a natural point of contact; themes included knowledge gaps, motivators for seeking information, and desired educational content.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports the needs-assessment/participant-voice premise underlying affected-person visibility (safeguard) and P2: independent qualitative evidence that couples at premarital counseling touchpoints (including faith-based sites) have specific, articulable information needs beyond what standard premarital counseling covers -- reinforces the case for content and process gaps that a governance-aware programme could address, though this study concerns reproductive/conception content specifically, not decision-control or coercion recognition.

records.title: Effect of Premarital Education on the Quality of Life of Female Partners: A Cross-Sectional Study.
records.design: Cross-sectional study (N=596 Saudi women married <=15 years)
records.population_setting: Saudi women, general population, Muslim-majority context
records.key_finding: Only 37.2% of participants had received premarital counseling/education, although 86.4% believed it was crucial before marriage; women who received premarital education/counseling and rated it as impactful had significantly higher WHOQOL-BREF quality-of-life scores.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly relevant background evidence for a Muslim-majority premarital-education context (though Saudi rather than Thai): documents a large gap between perceived importance (86.4%) and actual uptake (37.2%) of premarital education, supporting the rationale for scaling programmes like T-PHE in comparable settings; however, the cross-sectional, self-selected design cannot establish that education caused the quality-of-life association, and the outcome measured is general quality of life, not decision control, coercion recognition, or safe help-seeking -- illustrates the FAILURE CRITERION gap again (a positive conventional-outcome association says nothing about the governance-specific outcomes T-PHE targets).
records.evidence_level: Cross-sectional survey; associative, self-report, no control group

gaps_noted: No PubMed-indexed study was found that evaluates a premarital or marriage education programme against decision-control, coercion-recognition, or informed-choice outcomes as primary endpoints (the specific outcome domain the FAILURE CRITERION targets) -- every effectiveness study located, including the Hawkins/ACF meta-analyses, measures satisfaction, communication skills, relationship stability, or quality of life instead.

No PubMed-indexed evaluation of a STOP RULE-type screen-and-defer mechanism for suspected coercion/violence within premarital (as opposed to couple/marital) education specifically was found; the strongest supporting evidence (Markman 2013 PMID 23421844; Williamson 2015 PMID 25664643) is indirect, showing that joint relationship education can worsen outcomes for high-aggression/high-risk couples, not a direct test of a stop-and-refer protocol.

No Thailand-specific or Southeast Asian premarital/marriage education outcome study was located; the closest cultural analogues found are Iranian (PMID 40783649), Turkish (PMID 42442188), Saudi (PMID 36620784) and South Korean (PMID 39757299) studies -- none are Southeast Asian or specifically Thai Muslim/intercultural populations.

No PubMed-indexed premarital-education outcome study directly measures 'referral timeliness, accessibility, and follow-through' (P5) as a composite outcome; Williamson 2019 (PMID 30489129) and Williamson 2014 (PMID 24294929) are the closest available evidence, addressing help-seeking barriers and gateway effects respectively, but neither evaluates an actual referral pathway or its quality.

Very few identified studies use randomization with adequate power; several of the most contextually relevant recent studies (Iranian, Turkish) are small pilot/quasi-experimental trials (n=20-16 couples), limiting confidence in effect estimates even for conventional outcomes.

No meta-analysis or systematic review specifically on faith-based/religious-leader-delivered premarital education and safety/coercion outcomes was found via the systematic-review-filtered queries (query 2 returned 0 hits on the exact phrasing tried); this may reflect true absence of such reviews in PubMed rather than a search-term failure, but should not be treated as confirmed absence without a broader grey-literature search outside PubMed's scope.
limits_of_this_search: Search was restricted to PubMed via NCBI E-utilities only, per hard constraints; no WHO/UN/USPSTF/Cochrane full-text database, PsycINFO, or grey literature was searched, so meta-analyses/programmes only indexed in psychology-specific or non-PubMed databases (e.g., some PREP/marriage-education literature lives primarily in PsycINFO) may be under-represented despite PubMed's partial MEDLINE overlap with psychology journals. Search terms focused on relationship/marriage EDUCATION and its outcomes (per assigned angle); the much larger PubMed literature on premarital GENETIC/disease SCREENING (thalassemia, consanguinity, HIV, hepatitis) was deliberately excluded as out of this angle's scope even though many such records appeared in the initial pooled search (124 unique PMIDs across 8 queries) -- that screening literature is presumably covered by a different angle's search. All abstracts were read via efetch before being summarized; no full-text articles were accessed. Several older records (pre-2000) were retained because they represent the historical evidence base the modern MRE meta-analyses (Hawkins et al.) are built on, but their methodology is dated and should be weighted accordingly.
